Lockers drifted like battering rams. Ceiling panels dropped seemingly at random. A pipe blew just above Leon’s head, vapor hissing out before water collapsed down like a fist. He ducked, snarling, shaking it off. The school wasn't trying to just drown them anymore. It was trying to tire them out first. The alcove appeared near the end of the hallway, as Danny had predicted. Orela's beam caught the edge of it mid-stroke — a break in the wall, barely three feet across, tucked into the corridor like the building had forgotten to fill it in. One side was boarded up, the planks swollen and dark, water seeping through the gaps in thin steady threads that ran the wrong direction. Not draining out. Coming in, as if the entire building had gone under and the pressure outside was simply looking for the path of least resistance. Every surge that rolled down the hallway made the planks flex, a subtle outward bow that suggested they had opinions about the situation and were getting louder about them. The roar was marginally less here, enough that they didn’t need to scream to be heard. Orela pushed Danny and Dwight back into the nearby wall, using her body to brace them. She swept the flashlight across the warped planks, reading them, then felt Leon's hand close around hers and take the light. He moved to the boards, running his palm across the grain, pressing at the edges, testing the flex. His jaw worked once as he bit down the urge to try and slam into it himself. Everyone had tried unsuccessfully to break one of these at some point in their time in the Fog, almost always hurting themselves in the process. The killers always made it look so easy. Leon swept the flashlight across the planks one more time, jaw set, and stepped back. He looked at Danny, gesturing to the blockage. “Think you can break it?” Danny looked at the planks. Looked at his own hands, still faintly trembling from the hallway. The robes were gone. The mask was gone. The terror radius, the cloak, all of it — gone. He'd been running on borrowed time since the moment the school flinched, and he knew what that meant better than any of them. The Entity's gifts came as a package. You didn't get to keep the strength while She took back everything else. Or at least, he was fairly sure you didn't. He had no way to know for certain because killers didn't lose their gifts. Killers didn't end up treading water in a flooding preschool wondering if they still worked. “I’m really not sure anymore.” Leon helped pull him into the alcove, bracing against the current as best he could so Danny didn’t get torn away on him. “Well, you’re the only one of us with the clearance card. And it’s not like we have other options here.” The alcove gave them maybe two feet of working space behind Danny, which wasn't much, but it was something. He braced his back against the opposite wall, assessed the planks, and tried not to think too hard about the specific question sitting in the middle of his chest. Technically they weren’t wrong. He'd broken killer walls before. Hundreds of times, probably — the muscle memory of it was there, the particular angle and force and follow-through. That part wasn't the problem. The problem was that everything else had already been taken back. If he didn’t have the Entity’s strength, he doubted his normal human strength would be enough to crack it, let alone break it. She hadn’t shown any signs that She intended to spare him, so why would She give him such an easy out? But what choice did he have? He couldn’t just wallow in his sudden abandonment when he was just as screwed as the survivors. He needed to be useful, which was a different thing entirely and required not having someone treating him like he was about to fall over. He could fall over later. Right now, he squared his hips to the wall, pulled his knee up, and drove his heel into the planks. The kick landed solid through the water drag, the impact rattling back up through his hip and spine, water spraying across him in a sharp burst that made him flinch. His shoulders cracked against the wall behind him, jostling his ribs and reminding him of just how many were likely cracked. The planks made an awful sound under the impact, but he could feel it through his leg. It hadn’t shifted. Danny gritted his teeth. He hadn’t felt abandoned before. Not really. Not until now. If he couldn’t get this wall open, what then? He could barely manage to stand in this current unaided. What if they realized he wasn’t worth the extra hands to keep afloat? Leon shifted his grip on Danny’s arm and he jerked it away, moving to try again. He didn't have the breath to explain it and didn't particularly want to — the reasoning was simple enough, if not flattering. He'd already been hauled out of a hallway once tonight. He'd already been stripped of his gear while he stood there and let it happen. He was not going to stand in an alcove and be held upright like something that needed managing while he tried to do the one useful thing left available to him. This couldn’t afford to fail. They were going to leave him to Her fury; he just knew it. He slammed his heel against the wood, harder.
